utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The examination by Mr. Bakrac will now continue. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone. Your Honours, now I would like to move on to a new topic, the organization of the chain of command in the Pristina Corps. His Honour Judge Chowhan during an examination of a previous witness proposed that it would be good to have an organizational chart, that this would assist you, and Mr. Lazarevic did produce a chart of the subordinate units. And as soon as it was completed, we gave it a 5D number, but it -- we actually -- we moved for the list to be amended to include this exhibit. We haven't got the decision yet, so now I will be guided by you whether we can use it, whether it could be given an IC number now and Mr. Lazarevic would confirm that this is a chart that he produced. It would be as if he had done it here in front of us. But at any rate, I will be guided by you, whatever you say is the best course of action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the e-court number?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 5D1370.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, do you have a problem with using this in e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't have an objection to that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we shall allow you to amend the Rule 65 ter list, and we shall use the version in e-court 5D1370.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: With regard to that particular motion to amend the list, there were two exhibits we did have an objection to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So your motion is granted to that extent and the other two matters will be determined separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, let us call up on our screens in e-court Exhibit 5D1370, and I would like you to comment on it and to explain to us what was the structure, the organization of the chain of command, and how it functioned in the Pristina Corps during the state of war.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The organization of the system of in Pristina Corps at the operational level was highly complex, as indicated by this chart. This is an organizational chart, and there's also the technical and security aspect of it. With the permission of the honourable Trial Chamber, let me explain this organizational chart. Right at the top of this chart, we have the command post of the Pristina Corps, it is indicated by the letters PrK, KM, that is the central, the core of the command, but this is just main command post of the Pristina Corps. Above it you see a rectangle, it is also light blue, this shows the forward command post of the 3rd Army, indicating that throughout the war at the Pristina Corps command post there was the command post -- the forward command post of the 3rd Army. It was set up and manned. Now I would like to draw your attention to light blue rectangles on this chart. These are all organizationally subordinate units to the corps, according to the peacetime establishment, before the war. And as you can see, there are four dark blue rectangles, these are the units that came into being when the state of war was declared; in other words, the peacetime establishment is not very different from the wartime establishment. The blue colours indicate that the corps had nine regiment brigade-level units. Their establishment designations are [Realtime transcript read in error "rely"] indicated here it had seven battalions, two companies, and one institution or installation. Indicated in red are the 12 units that reinforced the corps during the war pursuant to the decisions of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia and the 3rd Army commander. Now, as to what are those units that the corps was successively reinforced, this is indicated in the rectangles, their decisions are there, and if necessary I will give you their names. Now let me explain the green colour. The green colour indicates the coordination with the units that are outside of the composition of the corps, it's the Nis Corps, the Podgorica Corps, the defence administration of the Ministry of Defence, air force and defence, Ministry of the Interior, the units in Kosovo, a helicopter squadron, an army artillery group, and a 52nd corps stationary communications centre. So these units are not part of the chain of the command, they are not subordinated to the corps command, but during the war there was coordination with those units. Right at the top of this chart you have two violet, two purple rectangles, indicating two commands. One is linked with the forward command post of the 3rd Army, that's the forward command post of the air force corps; and VoV indicates the air force liaison officers, they are linked with the Pristina Corps command. This is what we were talking about the combined combat operations in anti-aircraft defence, so there is no subordination there in this relationship. Let me conclude, the Pristina Corps had under its command in direct link -- it was directly linked with it, as you can see if we discount the purple rectangles and the green rectangles, it had about 30 units that were directly under the command of the Pristina Corps commander and his organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, let me just make this clear. I made a mistake. We will have a translation later on. This is the chain of command chart and the coordination chart for the Pristina Corps in the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now move on to exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't understand it at all, so I would be needed to be guided a little. The line which is L-shaped, if you had a bigger piece of paper would that be a straight line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, it could be drawn that way, in a straight line, but the important part is that there is a solid black line leading from the top going horizontally and then downwards. This indicates the chain of command, that the units that are along this line are subordinated to the corps command. The broken lines leading to the purple rectangles and the green rectangles indicate that there was no subordination. These units were not part of the Pristina Corps chain of command, they were not subordinated to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sure the hope was that you could demonstrate more than that by the diagram. The red rectangles, are they all at the same level? Are they all effectively directly connected to this black line which goes across and then becomes L-shaped? In other words, they should all be side by side, should they, if you had a bigger piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. These are all brigade-level units, the Pristina Military District units, that were subordinated to the Pristina Corps during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And if we go up one level, there's another black line with two dark blue rectangles and six light blue rectangles. What are they representing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the left, on the left-hand side of this chart, we have the units that are linked to the Pristina Corps command and the elements of command. Let me explain. The first light blue rectangle is the temporary Pristina garrison command. It took care of the smaller corps elements in the town of Pristina, we have the club and the orchestra, and it also provided accommodation for the military court and the military prosecutor's office. To the right, we have the elements of the command post. In addition to the main command post we established the logistics command post, the next command post, the centre for automatic surveillance of air-space, and other elements in the system of command, but we will be discussing that in detail later on through some other exhibits because this couldn't be depicted on this chart, all of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I had one final question, I've lost the part in the transcript. Yes, you said the blue colours indicate the corps had nine - let me see the exact wording - nine regiment brigade-level units, their establishment designations rely --- English translation - rely indicated here it had seven battalions, two companies, and one institution installation, in English that is gobbledygook. You must have said something different in B/C/S. Can we have this clarified, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's remark: We said are all indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, you heard the question from His Honour, could you please explain.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, definitely. The first nine rectangles in light blue below the thick horizontal line are establishment units at the brigade regiment level in the corps. There were nine brigades in the establishment and organization of the chart -- of the corps, from 125th Motorised Brigade and then onwards. And to the left, you can see lower-level units, battalion-level units, three border battalions are the first ones; then we have the military police battalion; two new battalions that were added in the war, additional battalion and the medical battalion; then we have the communications battalion. As you can see, there are seven battalions in the corps and nine brigades. Then there were also two companies, the 52nd Reconnaissance and Sabotage Company and the 52nd Electronic Reconnaissance Company, and there was also a unit from the military medical centre in Pristina. These are all the units that belonged to the Pristina Corps in peace and in wartime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, let us now move on to Exhibit 5D342. This is your order dated the 29th of March and it pertains to an attempt to ensure that the work and the commanding in the units of the corps should proceed in an undisrupted manner. Could you please explain to us what this is all about?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order that was drafted right at the beginning of the war in which I defined the division of command of the corps into several teams, groups, or elements, in accordance with the Rules of Combat and also as demanded by the situation, the general objective being that the chain of command should remain intact during the war because if the whole of the command post were to be located in a single sight with all its elements, it could be destroyed with a single strike. You can see here that the corps command was divided into the first part, the main command post which was manned by me and the part of the staff; then the second part was the logistics; the third part was the operations centre, the surveillance and warning centre; and the fourth part was the one that had to do with the creation of the military court and the prosecutor's office in the city of Pristina. As you can see here, the forward command post is not listed here because it was located in Djakovica even before the war but it was a command group until the Chief of Staff went there to man that post. At least five parts of the Pristina Corps command were located all over Kosovo and Metohija, which means that I -- my command was not located in a single site but in at least five different sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, could you please look at 5D348, again this is a document from the Pristina Corps command, the date is the 30th, a day after the one that we just looked at, and could you please explain to us what is this order all about.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order also indicates that in the initial period during the war exceptional efforts were made to make sure the chain of command survived the initial strikes because the system of command was the first to be targeted in the NATO air-strikes. I issued a decision that a group from the corps command be formed to temporarily command the garrison in Pristina and take care of those smaller non-combat units, the military library, the military orchestra, the headquarters command, the centre for information, the various employees on the ground, and to ensure there was a military court and military prosecutor's office at the corps command. This was an additional group which was in the Pristina garrison all the time and certain people were designated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We'll come to that, General. Colonel Milutin Filipovic was the group leader and he will testify, he is our second witness after you. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was an assistant for personnel, affairs in the corps command, and he was the group leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please, where was this group located in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was located in several buildings, military or socially owned facilities, in the Pristina area or, quite simply, in the town of Pristina but on several locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You mentioned the military prosecutor's office and the military court. We'll come to that, but what were the powers of this group in relation to the military court and prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This command group was duty-bound to create the materiel, logistical, and organizational prerequisites for the military court and military prosecutor's office to be put in place and secured from any possible attacks by terrorist forces in Pristina. They had to create the necessary security conditions for them, the technical, materiel, and logistical conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. In the course of the war, from the beginning of the air-strikes onwards, were there any factors limiting the functioning of the system of command?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, the chain or system of command from the high strategic level, the General Staff of the third level, especially down to the corps command, was the first to be targeted, both by NATO air-strikes and long-distance strikes, and this meant that the security conditions were extremely complex and extremely limiting. In the chart we showed here, I tried to show that the chain of command was very complex. There were over 30 units which were resubordinated to the corps command in wartime, and according to military doctrine we have heard Defence witnesses testifying for General Ojdanic who said that the norm would be six to eight or ten such links at the most. As regards telecommunications and technical conditions, these posed a strategic problem for the command system.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said six to eight lines of communication or links. How many lines of communication did you have, as we have just heard the norm would be six to eight, how many lines of communication did you have?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, ten at the most would be the norm, but here we have seen there were 30 or 35.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And you had to do that in the war?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was done in the way I have described.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, how was the system of combat reporting regulated in the corps?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have Exhibit 5D351 brought up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The system of combat reporting in the corps command was defined in accordance with the order issued by the 3rd Army command and the General Staff according to a single principle, a single order. There was only one method according to which daily combat reports were compiled. We see on the screen an order issued by the Pristina Corps command dated the 31st of March, where I draw attention to the fact that over the past few days a small number of units delivered daily combat reports because of the intensity of the fighting. I refer to the order issued by the army command and I demand that combat reports be submitted every day as of 1500 hours on that day, and then interim reports as needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you order that attempts be made to call by telephone -- to call the command?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we have 5D362.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regardless of this order - and there were several orders dealing with the issue of combat reporting - the chain of command was limited to a large extent. And very often combat reports arrived late or did not arrive at all because of technical difficulties. I decided on the 4th of April to attempt to order additional reporting by telephone. The subordinate commanders were to call the corps command or the operations centre and tell them briefly if the lines were not jammed, to inform them about the situation in the units. This is the order in which I first of all warned that daily combat reports are not arriving, that there are numerous difficulties, I'm aware of the difficulties, but I require if there is no written report that the commanders at least call the corps operations centre and tell them the main points regarding the situation in the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, how did this reporting by telephone function? Were there difficulties in this respect?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even in the brief periods of time when the communications system was operating properly in technical terms, it was often jammed so that it would happen that for days on end there were no telephone communications with certain units. And this caused huge problems, including defeatism in some brigades. They didn't know what was going on, and some commanders used a roundabout telecommunications system, asking that they be permitted to come to the command centre to meet me and to tell me what was happening in the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, how was the duty service organized in the Pristina Corps and its subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we have 5D200 brought up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was the third attempt, the third way in which an attempt was made for the system of command to the greatest possible extent in those wartime conditions to have its basic functions; and in accordance with the Rules of Service of the Army of Yugoslavia and the situation on the ground, I ordered that continual duty be organized, regardless of the situation with telephones, when they were operating and when they were not operating. So if they started operating, even if it was only for half an hour, there would be somebody there to respond. And also whenever an air threat was announced, whenever there was a warning, the commands had to leave the operative centres or the places where the telephones and comm systems were in place and to take shelter. So as long as there was an air-raid alert, these could not function, communications could not function. I said that there had to be someone next to the telephone, not a private but an officer, in spite of the danger there had to be someone by the phone always ready to answer. That's the gist of this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, this monitoring of the situation in the units and the system of command and telecommunications, was this a strategic problem in implementing the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was an insuperable strategic problem throughout the war, and it gave rise to grave concerns, both on the part of the army commander who was distraught, and he asked me how we were going to get through all of that, how they were going to endure it. And because I dealt with these issues on a daily basis I told him out of the 78 days of the war, 56 days were days in which the system of command seen from the aspect of reporting and monitoring the situation in the units was not [as interpreted] functioning properly or was functioning 30 per cent. The rest of the time it was not functioning, so we were reduced to the level of World War I and we sent off couriers; that was our method of communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, was there any need for frequent changes of the location of the command post, the command of the Pristina Corps where you were?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a need not only in the tactical sense, but it was a matter of survival in order to avoid casualties and to survive the wartime conditions. The corps command, I'm referring to the main command post and all the others as well, moved every other day, at least every other day, and changed its location.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, 5D349, it seems that this is indicated here in this document, so these frequent relocations along with the technical problems were giving rise to all the problems we have been discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have this document brought up, please, 5D349.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this document, the 3rd Army command on the 31st of March, 1999, is reporting to the Supreme Command Staff, the operative administration, saying that there are intensified combat operations, increasingly frequent ground and air attacks, that the commands are constantly relocating, and that all this, especially in the Pristina Corps, is making difficult secure communications and is causing difficulties in gathering and processing in a reliable way information on the situation in the units. The Supreme Command Staff is also being informed that everything is being done to stabilize the system, but the situation is such as it is and there are no -- there's no information from the units, so that will be delivered later.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, let's look at two more documents very quickly and we'll move on, 5D359, dated the 2nd of April, please, this seems to be a document compiled by you. So can we please look at the last item on the first page. You are complaining here, it seems, that measures are not being taken to re-establish severed communication lines. Let's see what this is about, it's dated the 2nd of April, and it's addressed to the commander.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I sent this document to the subordinate commanders, not to complain to them but to draw attention to the numerous problems regarding the functioning of the system of command. Quite simply, I concluded and I informed the commanders of this that all this is creating problems at the level of the corps command when decisions have to be made. In this last sentence I remind them, the last sentence of the first page, that according to the Rules of Combat subordinate units are duty-bound to make efforts to establish telecommunications with their superior units if these have been disrupted. So the basic rule is that the superior had to establish the system in relation to the subordinates, but it also applies vice versa.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. And let us now look at the last document dealing with this topic, this is your combat report dated the 13th of April, and could you please comment on item 6, command and communications. That's the last page, page 3, or rather, it's page 3 of 4 -- I'm sorry, it's -- it's a Prosecution exhibit, P2004, item 6, command and communications. The number of the document is P2004. Okay we see it in front of us, item 6, General, please. This is a document dated the 13th of April. It appears that some kind of contact had been established by some of the units only at that time, so therefore there had been no contact, but could you please comment on item 6, please.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a combat report of the Pristina Corps command sent to the Supreme Command Staff and the 3rd Army, and I just wanted to remind the Court that last week we said that on the 11th and the 12th and onwards, in fact, were the dates when the air-strikes and long-range strikes had become very intensive. And on the 13th, communication lines with all the units were down. And now I am reporting - let me read - "communications have been accomplished with all the units," so on day three we were able to establish the communications with the exception, and then I list four brigades, that on the third day and onwards remained incommunicado. And because of constant danger and missile strikes, the encryption of the data has been disrupted and reporting -- reports come in late throughout the corps. Encryption means that the reports are sent in an encrypted form because this is the only way in which you can actually send data during the war, and such combat reports were sent on every second or third day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did the Pristina Corps establish any kind of information centre and what were the possibilities actually to do so given the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the public media, the press and the electronic media, in Kosovo and Metohija were not available to the commands and the units because they were not functioning, all the transmission systems were down with the exception of the foreign satellite channels, a decision was made at the level of the Supreme Command Staff and later on at the level of the 3rd Army to reinforce the Pristina Corps with a group of officers from the General Staff who would become part of the composition of the corps and would set up an information centre, so to speak, in the basement of the Grand Hotel. Many witnesses referred to it as the corps command post, but this was not so; this was the information centre of the Pristina Corps. And their task, the task of this group of people, was to communicate with the media centre in Pristina, to communicate with the hundreds of relatives of the soldiers; and the information it gathered was then to be relayed to the units. In those circumstances, the corps command asked for battery-operated radio stations to be distributed to the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you explain to us, what was the position of the Pristina Corps in the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would just like to tell you that the chain of command in the corps and with the corps from the 3rd Army and the Supreme Command was intact and it was in line with all the Rules of Combat and the principles of command in the Army of Yugoslavia. Let me remind you once again, Your Honours, that as far as I know this was a rare occasion in practice for a strategic command such as the army command to be located at the command post of a corps throughout the war so close to the front line. And let me conclude that not a single day, not a single day went by without the presence of the army commander at the command post of the Pristina Corps. All the orders, all the decisions, all the amendments to the orders were sent from the army command to the corps command and then further down the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your answer has been translated into English as saying that: "The chain of command was intact both down through the corps and up to the 3rd Army and the Supreme Command." Now, it's absolutely clear what you're saying about the 3rd Army and the Supreme Command. Are you also saying, following all the answers you've just given, that the chain of command down through the corps was intact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, that is what I meant to say, and if there is any imprecision let me just say that the brigade commanders were in command of their subordinate units and the corps command commanded the brigades. And the 3rd Army command commanded the corps and then further up, that's the whole chain of command. I wanted to cut this long story short, but I wanted to say precisely what you have just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But if I understand His Honour the Presiding Judge correctly, in light -- in spite of all the difficulties and problems that you just enumerated?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I spoke at length about those substantial strategic problems, but in my last answer I just wanted to say that despite all that the chain of command was in line with the rules. Whenever it was possible to issue commands or orders, it was done. There were no departures from this chain of command, as we have come to call it here, of the subordination system.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, we have seen that in your orders you insist on the compliance with the Geneva Conventions and humane treatment of the civilian population. Now I want to know whether the lower units included those provisions in their orders, including the reserve units.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All the subordinate commands strictly complied with the orders issued from the corps command in terms of provisions and acting upon those provisions. But before the war started, such measures were already defined in case the war started.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at 5D477, that is an order from the 354th Infantry Brigade, the date is the 4th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And the reference is to one of your orders dated the 2nd of February. Could we please look at it and could you please comment on item 8.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please not overlap with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 5D477. Could we look at item 8, which is on page 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In February training of the reserve force was done in the corps units. It lasted a couple of days. This was in line with the yearly training plan for the reserve force. This brigade was deployed in the Kursumlija garrison outside of Kosovo and Metohija, it was subordinated to the corps command under the organizational chart. And on the 2nd of February, 1999, I ordered that when the reserve elements in this brigade are trained, that the whole of the brigade should be familiarised with the provisions of the Geneva Conventions and the way in which the captured and wounded members of the enemy forces are to be treated. This is the last sentence in item 8. So the reserve force, if it were ever to be used, should be informed as to what they should do in terms of combat -- conduct in combat and the compliance with the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And on the 12th of March, that's 5D260, Exhibit 5D260, a document that deals with the maintenance and improvement of combat-readiness, you say that if there were any conflicts that you actually order some preventive measures. Could you please look at item 5 in this document and tell us if that is indeed so.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Last week I testified that in February and March the functioning of the Pristina Corps was organized in this manner. Every week there were briefings, and this is one such document. It pertains to the week of the 13th to the 19th of March, 1999, and I demand after this briefing by the subordinate commanders that any enemy but also criminal and other activities in all the units of the corps should be uncovered and prevented promptly in a systematic matter and that all the perpetrators should be punished either by disciplinary measures or should even be criminally prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, was every soldier given some kind of a pocket edition of the Rules of Conduct in Combat, and could we please have Exhibit 5D199 and if you could confirm if this is what we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As early as in June 1998 a form was sent down from the General Staff, it was a pocket laminated brochure, it is called the Rules of Conduct in Combat. It was designed for the troops, and as soon as a soldier came to the corps or a brigade, we issued this to those soldiers and we demanded that it be studied carefully. We can see the last pages here on the screen. There are -- there's one or two more pages, and in an appropriate manner they instruct the fighters, the soldiers, how to treat the civilians, how to treat the enemy soldiers, how to treat property so that really every soldier had it in his pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, you say that this document contains some other pages. I assume that they are on the back of these pages, and could you please tell us does this fold up in some way, in three parts, so that it can be put in the blouse pocket?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, it folds up like an accordion, this is just one part of it but that's the size of it. You can fit it into the blouse pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did the Pristina Corps command issue any instructions as to the disciplinary and criminal responsibility and the compliance with the Rules of Service of the Army of Yugoslavia as soon as the war started?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we please have Exhibit 5D332 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can remember, on the second or even first day of the war -- on the second day of the war the corps command issued an order and an instruction on taking an application of measures of disciplinary and criminal responsibility in compliance with the Rules of Service of the Army of Yugoslavia in wartime. This is dated the 25th of March. It is an order which I sent in a form of a telegram to all the units demanding that in spite of the state of war disciplinary responsibility in war should -- in wartime should be done in -- as it is usually done, and criminal responsibility is to be dealt with by the military prosecutor's office and the military court at the Pristina Corps and the military district that was set up later. I also demanded all the Rules of Service be complied with. I instruct the subordinate commanders to refer to the Law on Defence, this is last couple of items, telling them how to apply some of the provisions of the Law on Defence, the provisions regarding the security regime in their areas of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In this document did you give any instructions regarding the restrictions of the freedom of movement and the conditions in which this is to be imposed?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not specifically describe it, but as you can see in the last-but-one passage, the last sentence reads that -- I demand from the commanders to act in accordance with the Article 70, paragraph 2 of the Law on Defence. As far as I am able to paraphrase this article without having actually now to quote from it, it says that in wartime conditions, officers at the level of the brigade commander have the right and the duty in the combat zone to restrict temporarily the movement of all persons to prevent them from entering the combat zone. This is the essence of this last sentence in the penultimate paragraph, that's Article 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And further on during the first days of the war, the command of the 3rd Army and the Pristina Corps, or rather, they issued specific orders to their subordinate units on the specific application of international humanitarian law; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 5D1144, dated the 2nd of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The command of the 52nd Artillery Brigade. And it seems that this order is based on yet another order of yours dated the 29th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wish to say to the honourable Trial Chamber that every two or three days there would be a special order in terms of observing Rules of Conduct and international humanitarian law, and these were addressed to subordinate commanders. Of course the corps command received numerous orders of this nature and the corps command itself took initiatives in this domain. What you are referring to is an order of the commander of the 52nd Artillery Rocket Brigade of the PVO dated the 2nd of April, where he refers to my order of the 29th of March, 1999, and he orders all his subordinate units to fully comply with the instructions on the observance of the rules of international humanitarian law and he says who was responsible for this application. He defines the particular role of the security organs in respect of these measures. He calls on the commanders to report to him on the consistent implementation of that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do apologise. In order to move on faster I omitted one document along the same lines, the 23rd of March, I'm not going to open it, but I just wish to refer to it, it's 5D1293. It doesn't have to be opened, I'm just referring to it. I just want to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to this. Could we now have a look at 5D1000.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can we hear your comments as to whether the command of the military district issued such orders.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that all subordinate units, and there's no doubt about that, had to act in accordance with the orders of the corps command. Here the military district was at that time subordinated to the command of the 3rd Army and it acted in accordance with the orders of the command of that army in terms of carrying out these measures, here specifically in relation to the prohibition of criminal behaviour vis-a-vis the property of citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in this respect I wish to refer to document 5D343, dated the 29th of March, 1999; and P2029 dated the 1st of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, please, you said that practically every two or three days -- well, let's have a look at this document dated the 5th of April. We did not open all of them, we just invoked some of them. So 5D365. I think this is your document and I think that you wrote it on the basis of the initials there, so could we hear your brief comments.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I compiled this order as the corps commander, with a view to decidedly for the umpteenth time, this was only ten days into the war or 12 days into the war, once again I wish to issue an order to the commanders to strictly adhere to the security regiment; that is to say in coordination with the MUP of the Republic of Serbia and the civilian protection they should protect the units, the war materiel reserves, to help in protecting law and order, and especially the civilian population. Also, that they help the MUP forces in the return of displaced persons. And in all of this, they should abide by all the orders pertaining to the Rules of Service of the Army of Yugoslavia and observing international humanitarian law.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we also wish to refer to 5D803 dated the 16th of April, subordinate brigades, pertaining to the order of the Pristina Corps to the same effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, we have already seen that in the general order for the defence of the country, Grom 4, that is document 175, in the combat orders, in the orders for controlling territory. And now in the last orders you always cautioned that international laws of war should be applied properly and that the civilian population should be treated properly. We see that this pertains to the return of the population, taking care of them, providing them with food. Were there any attempts made by you in terms of efforts, measures to have part of the medical battalion take part in providing assistance to the civilian population. I would like to call-up 5D592, please.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Practically, there is not a single combat order. There is not any order for stabilizing defence or any other order where emphasis is not laid on the attitude of corps members towards observing humanitarian law with a focus on the civilian population. I wish to say to the honourable Trial Chamber that the corps as an operational unit that defends the country in terms of the focus of its defence does not have special tasks that it would be the protagonist of taking care of civilian population in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, but indeed we did everything we possibly could to help wherever possible the civilian population to survive or to return and stay as safe as possible. It is in that sense that I order the medical battalion that is supposed to provide medical support to the corps to use all their resources to aid the civilian population in the broader area of Podujevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: On the screen we have an order of the commander of the 211th Armoured Brigade. It pertains precisely to what you've been telling us about now, but we see that he invokes the order of the Pristina Corps dated the 16th of April and the number is there as well. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is just one part. This order of mine of the 16th of April, well with the permission of the honourable Trial Chamber I explain that this is a rather special order by which I ordered to practically establish elements in every brigade that would take care. So this would not only be on paper, these would be forces that would take care of the civilian population, and the commander of the 211th Armoured Brigade established a unit from the ranks of the engineering battalion, from the medical unit too, to take care of the displaced population in the area of Lab and the Podujevo municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, we saw your orders. You saw that lower-ranking units incorporated your orders into their own orders. Did you caution lower-ranking units about that, that your orders should be carried out in this way?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So let us have a look at 5D198.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Generally speaking, the method of work of the corps command after the issuing of such orders and tasks was to follow as much as possible whether this was indeed being implemented on the ground. So what followed were these warnings, these reminders of these orders, as well as personal inspection on my part and on the part of the commander of the army. We were trying to look into the matter to see how this was being carried out in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, we'll have a look at that quickly, too, but let us look at this document now. It seems to be a document of yours dated the 18th of April. It is sent to the commanders and it says that according to some information there were individual cases of behaviour in combat operations which were inappropriate. And is this a warning yet again?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The corps command received some information beforehand that there had been individual cases of an improper attitude on the part of individuals from the brigade vis-a-vis the civilian population in terms of the property of these civilians, some of their property was stolen. After the warning that came from the army command, I warn commanders that they should fully, in all respects, abide by all the orders issued and the instructions from the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, all the orders of the corps command, and that there should be no deviation from these orders in terms of their implementation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, the date is the 18th of April. It seems that immediately on the 19th the subordinate commands sent this further down, 5D805 is the document, the command of the 7th Infantry Brigade. It seems that they are also invoking your warning and issuing their order to lower-ranking units and cautioning them to respect all of this. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These warnings from the corps command do not pertain to all units. It's not that all units were affected, but whenever something would happen anywhere, warnings would be issued to all units. And this brigade commander is invoking my order of the 18th of April, and the number is there too, and he is cautioning his subordinated that they should strictly observe all the orders issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I just wish to intervene for -- I'm sorry, General, to ask this, to raise this query. Now, there were repeated orders, there were inspections, and there were cases. I mean, because there was -- there were repeated cases of violation of your orders, is that the reason that you kept on sending the orders again and again? I mean, there must have been many cases which necessitated the disposition of this order. What have you to say. And secondly, I wanted to ask you what did you mean by improper attitude, because very vague term. I shall be very grateful if you'll kindly answer this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with all due respect, I would not say that there were major phenomena of lack of observance of orders, violations of rules, violations of international humanitarian law. I wish to say, because I drafted these orders too and the army commander, next to who I was all the time, quite simply in a preventive manner, every day, consistently, that we should take preventive action vis-a-vis subordinate units. And then there is specific -- a specific reference in this order that specific things happened, that property was stolen, that there was looting, property of civilians, and this is in violation of the orders that had been issued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: And, General, sorry, what did you mean by improper attitude? Can you define it, where it looks a bit vague, I couldn't understand it, you used the word in your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For me as a commander, even the mildest form of excessive behaviour, namely, that a soldier stops a civilian or a group of civilians in an unauthorised manner, that is improper, that is impermissible behaviour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in terms of having these measures taken, I would like to draw your attention to 5D201, dated the 19th of April, it is a document of the corps command, with a view to taking care of the civilian population that was on the move; and 5D372, dated the 22nd of April, 1999, also issued by the command of the Pristina Corps in which what is insisted upon is the accelerated return of the civilian population that is returning to its villages and towns; also Exhibit 5D374, dated the 23rd of April, 1999; also 5D1291, in which the command of the 7th Infantry Brigade on the 23rd of April further orders the subordinate units to secure and look after and accommodate the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, from the subordinate brigades did you receive reports as to what was done in relation to the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The order of the corps command and my order in a special item required that the subordinate commands on a regular basis include in their daily combat reports what they did and how pursuant to these orders. And the brigades reported on all the measures undertaken to implement these orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Before we move on to show a few example, please look at 5D389 of the 2nd of May, 1999, where it seems you again refer to orders already issued and where you again insist that the civilian population be looked after, accommodated in suitable buildings and not left out in the open.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I drafted this order personally. I issued a similar order on the 19th of April where I required that all possible assistance be given to the civilian population, the civilian authorities, and the civilian protection which was dealing with these issues, also the MUP forces involved in this humane work. And now after ten days and more, I'm again requiring of the commanders that they continue with these activities wherever they can to take in the civilian population, protect it, and provide it with all possible assistance. So this is not about deviations or failure to comply with orders, but it's about the insistence of the corps command to assist the civilian population wherever possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, let's briefly go through a few documents before the break as regards what was done. Please look at 5D793, here the commander of the 7th Infantry Brigade is informing you on the 4th of May that measures have been taken to assist the civilian population. Can we quickly comment on this and two other documents, and then we'll simply list the remaining ones.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's the gist of this response and the previous one. The brigade commander is informing me about what was done in Istok municipality or Istok town and Klina town where everything was done for the civilian population, the unit provided assistance, and he is responding to my query. He says that wherever possible, wherever there are no terrorist forces attacking the unit, the newly arrived civilian population returnees and displaced persons are being provided with assistance and security. So this is an example of compliance with my order on the part of a brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Please look at 5D1103, that is a combat report of the 52nd Brigade dated the 4th of May, 1999, and please look at item 11, miscellaneous or other. It seems that in this brigade's area of responsibility there were no civilian refugees, although there were many civilians in Gnjilane?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we see two different approaches here. One commander in a special document reported to the corps command, saying that there was several locations where the civilian population was located, and here the commander of the 52nd Mixed Artillery Brigade is reporting to me within his regular daily combat report, referring to my previous order of the 2nd of May, and reporting that in his area of responsibility there are no displaced persons out in the open and that the town of Gnjilane is full of civilians and that these civilians have the basic necessities.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, can we now look at two more documents concern -- these documents refer to the medical battalion. Please look at 5D1104, this is a report from the command of the 52nd Medical Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the translation of this document has not arrived yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you please briefly comment, Witness, what you reported or what you were informed of here?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the medical battalion of the Pristina Corps, Dr. Disic is here informing me that in the surgical station of the medical battalion assistance was provided to two persons, two civilians of Albanian ethnicity, that their injuries were a consequence of NATO air-strikes, also that a tour was made of, as it says here, a refugee camp in the village of Metohija, where returnees had come back and that measures had been proposed to the Podujevo Crisis Staff to improve assistance to that civilian population in order to prevent epidemics. And to the best of my recollection, he later reported that the medical battalion also got involved by distributing medicines to the civilian medical organs and helped accommodate women and children in the Podujevo area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: PD1109 [as interpreted], please. This is dated the 22nd of May, and it shows what the medical battalion did in item 9 under (a), it seems that they also are reporting that refugees are returning to their houses.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we please have the Serbian version brought back. Dr. Disic, the commander of the medical battalion, is reporting to me that seven babies in the village of Metohija have been taken care of, that there have been three interventions, one heart attack, and two sprained ankles, and this was -- this assistance was provided to civilians. He is also informing me that there is a danger of terrorist attacks against the medical battalion, that it does not have enough security, that even though the doctors are going out amongst the civilians, among the civilians there are members of the terrorist forces. And he is asking for assistance, asking how those medical teams providing assistance to the civilian population out on the ground can be better protected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, can we break now or is there something in particular you want to --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was just about, but there are just two other documents I wish to refer to and then I would suggest a break, 5D509 of the 1st of May, 1999; and 5D390 of the 4th of May, 1999, are similar documents demonstrating the same point. And now, Your Honour, it is a convenient moment for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we'll break now and resume just after ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Before the break I mentioned -- I omitted to mention 5D236, a combat report of the Pristina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, last week we spoke about prisoners taken by the KLA terrorist forces. Were there any and where were they located, and please look at document 5D368 dated the 4th of April, 1999, it's a short document, please comment on it.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Last week I answered the question put to me to the best of my knowledge and based on the combat reports there were 215 members of the terrorist forces who had been taken prisoner by the corps units, and these prisoners of war, after a brief prescribed procedure, the so-called security processing by the security service of the brigade and the corps were handed over to the competent MUP organs and then to the civilian judiciary. In the corps there was no collection centre or camp for prisoners of war. We have before us a document issued by the 3rd Army command, signed by the army Chief of Staff, addressed to the staff of the Supreme Command at the beginning of the war, reporting to the staff that in the army and the corps, in this organizational structure, there is no prisoner-of-war camp. So the proposal is made that prisoners of war should be evacuated to the area of the 1st Army out of the area of Kosovo and Metohija, where they would be safer and more secure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And what was done pursuant to this letter, do you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what I've already said, that prisoners of war taken by the corps members were processed through this procedure and then handed over to the MUP organs and the TO --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, the interpreter hasn't picked up what you're saying. Could you repeat that. We've got that: "The prisoners of war taken by corps members were processed through this procedure and then handed over to the MUP organs ..." We've already had all this evidence. I don't know if there's something else that is going to be added by going over it again, Mr. Bakrac. Is there some particular point that we haven't already dealt with on this subject?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. There will be a witness and we've already heard a protected witness who testified about the handover of some prisoners to the MUP. We feel that this question is important to demonstrate that there were no conditions in place to accommodate these prisoners, and we see a combat report here showing that they were handed over to the police organs. We will not dwell on this any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The real issue is why were there no facilities and what's the point in telling your army to obey all the rules of war and deal with everybody under the Geneva Convention properly and so on if you don't actually have the facilities? What we're getting from this evidence largely is a journey through the documentation without much evidence of what was actually happening on the ground. In any event, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. These documents show -- well, we'll come to that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, please look at PD522 [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I assume -- the English translation is PD, does that mean 5D or is it a Prosecution exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 5D522.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: This is a combat report of the 354th Infantry Brigade, showing that KLA members who had been taken prisoner were handed over to the police, this is the processing you mentioned, and then they were handed over to the MUP.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is concrete evidence of the manner of proceeding on the ground in wartime of subordinate units in compliance with orders of the corps command as to how international humanitarian law was to be respected in relation to prisoners. There are dozens of such reports but commanders will also come and testify here about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. What was the procedure followed by the Pristina Corps units with war booty. First explain what war booty is and then tell us what the procedure was.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the Rules of Combat of the Army of Yugoslavia and of other armed forces worldwide, war booty is a legitimate source of supply for units engaged in war. War booty means material resources of different kinds, which in the course of fighting has been taken from the enemy side. The entire procedure as regards war booty is defined in wartime by a number of orders from the General Staff to the army command, and then from there to the subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 5D188.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And if you could comment on it briefly. It seems to be an order issued by you in connection with war booty and confiscated vehicles. This order contains ten items, General. Could you just briefly tell us what this refers to and what it regulates.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order issued by the Pristina Corps command dated the 12th of April, 1999, in which the procedure as regards various resources which are war booty is regulated. This refers to food, consumer products, and other materials and weapons and ammunition and so on. It has to be received by a commission, recorded according to the instructions on material and financial proceedings and must not be misused by individuals. It must not be, in other words, taken, abused, or stolen by individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So each item had to be marked by the commission, it had to be safe-guarded?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can further clarify, it was important for the commission to establish what the war booty was, for it to be safe-guarded and stored, and part of the war booty could be used pursuant to a decision by the military court if, or rather, it might be part of a criminal proceeding or pursuant to a decision by the superior commander. So war booty had to be treated according to all the relevant regulations of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you explain the first paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the first paragraph the procedure is defined regarding food products and consumer goods that happened to be in the abandoned warehouses of the OSCE and the UNHCR in Pristina. Colonel Pesic, a Prosecution witness, testified about this, namely, that there was looting there, that these material resources were stolen, and that with part of his unit he secured that warehouse so that there would be no further theft. The corps command ordered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You have clarified one thing, which is that these were all abandoned warehouses. What was intended to be done with the aid and food that had been abandoned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This order is preceded by a special order regarding logistics security, precisely defining the inspection of these food products. If they are in proper condition, then the corps command allows, through its decision, to have such products be used by lower-ranking units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So they would be diverted away from their original destination of providing aid for refugees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot be specific on this, whether these resources were and what resources were exactly involved. It wasn't only food products that were given to refugees, but I know for sure, Mr. President, Your Honour, that soldiers gave some of their own food to the civilian population in areas where that civilian population happened to be. I hope that we will have occasion to hear the witnesses who are yet to come talk about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Well, I too have a question, and sorry for interruption. If we read the history of wars, obviously booty implies something which you take in other territory from the enemy. Here you were within your own geographical plains, and the property belonged to those people who were living there. I'm surprised how would you twist the classical meaning of booty to the one which has been stated today. This is one surprise which has come to me. And secondly, how can you treat this as a war booty when it has been taken from your own citizens or from warehouses where things were stored for various purposes? And how could you appropriate to yourself or to your soldiers things which belonged to the civilians? I mean, this is very, very strange. I'm sorry for this long question, but I think kindly elaborate, because I'm also astonished to see this order, Exhibit 5D188, why was there a necessity of issuing such an order and legitimizing what was happening, to take away this property and give it to the commanders? I mean, why was this happening? That's something you will have to kindly clarify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, Your Honour, may I say that either I did not sufficiently explain how this was interpreted or it is something else, but you did not understand me. War booty is not the property of the civilian population, but of the rebel terrorist forces that they used when fighting against their own state and the legitimate force of that state, specifically vehicles, various vehicles on which lethal weapons were mounted, then different medicines. Let me tell you quite openly, there were even drugs there and all sorts of things that were found and used by the terrorist forces. It's not that civilian organs or the civilian population were using this. War booty means that these resources were being used by the other side, the opposing side, and that is in agreement with combat rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: But, General, if you kindly read paragraph 6 of the order, this is something different than what you have kindly stated. I quite appreciate what you are trying to interpret, but what happens to paragraph 6 of your order, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I kindly ask you, Your Honour, that you look at the following. There are two things in the heading of this order: Procedure with seized and requisitioned goods. I focused here on war booty, but you are right. When this order - it is true - defines procedure with -- with other equipment, other resources that were either illegally seized or were found in the area of combat activities. And on page 2 of this document, procedure with such resources is defined, too, basically that they cannot be abused, that they cannot be taken away. Briefly, that is the procedure involved from paragraph 6. With the permission of the Trial Chamber, please take a look at paragraph 8. It says here that if some of the resources mentioned in this order were found before this date, everyone should act in accordance with this order. Under the control of commissions, nothing should be taken away, that it's the military court that decides how these items are to be used further. It is not for the commanders to decide on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You specifically refer to war booty as food products and consumer products. What do you mean by consumer products?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, as for consumer goods, among them there were usual communication devices, too, of a conventional nature, non-military, but they could be held -- used as hand-held radios for military purposes, too. Then TV sets, radio sets that were used by forces, terrorist forces, within their bases and strongholds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So, General, so that this be clear, you insisted here that all these goods that were taken away, that were seized, that were the subject of criminal behaviour, that they be recorded, stored, secured, and that they cannot be taken away, cannot be taken anywhere, is that the core of this order?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you understood it properly, and I explained to His Honour the Presiding Judge. War booty is one thing, and equipment that was illegitimately taken is a different matter, things that are the object of criminal offences. A special order refers to that. I give an order as to how one should act in accordance with the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Let us move on, General. Did you take measures with a view to preventing a lack of discipline and did you do this by yourself, through personal inspection?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a look at 5D384.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One of the ways to ensure the strict compliance with these orders is everyday insistence on military order and discipline, because if there is combat discipline, then it is more certain that these orders will be carried out. That is an answer to the first part of your question. As for the second part, certainly, whenever security conditions allowed for that, we tried to reach the units concerned and to see what their specific behaviour was and whether they were adhering to orders, the ones that we're discussing today, and others, pertaining to the security regimen and the implementation of tasks in general. Specifically, this is an order that I drafted on the 29th of April, 1999, when I carried out an unannounced inspection in the area of Drenica. And I saw that part of the unit of the 37th Motorised Brigade was in a position that was impermissible from the point of view of combat. They were exposed to NATO air-strikes. Soon a few of them would get killed. So I ordered the commander of the brigade on the basis of this personal insight of mine, that he urgently look into the responsibility of commanders and commanding officers who allowed this kind of violation of the security regimen during the course of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: On the same day, did you write an order of warning to all other brigades, 5D385?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In one of my previous answers I said that the system and method of work was that we take advantage of every single case or example to indicate this to other units so that other units would also act in accordance with orders issued. On that same day -- well, this was an order just for one brigade, but I personally on the same day drafted an order on the 29th of April, 1999, that would go to all units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 5D385, that is what it is, Your Honours. Could we please have a look at 5D1020 dated the 1st of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: It seems that the commander of the 37th Motorised Brigade is reacting to your warning of the 29th.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commanders of the 37th Motorised Brigade took this order of mine seriously, the one that was based on my personal insight. And in the last paragraph of the heading he recalls my order, my personal insight, and he unequivocally asks subordinate commanders to fully comply with all orders issues. So the brigade commanders is acting already on the next day, on that order of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, now that we're dealing with these documents, a few moments ago we saw from document 5D384 that on the 29th of April at 9.00 you personally came across part of the 37th Brigade near the village of Lozica. Can you tell us where the village of Lozica is and where it is in relation to Djakovica, where it is in Kosovo and in relation to Djakovica. I'm asking you this and I'm going to put two more questions to you in relation to the testimony of Nike Peraj who says he saw you in Djakovica when Meja took place on the 27th, 28th, and 29th, those were his words, he said that the action took place on those days.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village of Lozica is in the broader area of Klina, closer to the Drenica region, where the units of the 37th Motorised Brigade were. Around 9.00 I set out to tour and inspect in an unannounced manner, as I said, the 125th Brigade and the 37th Brigade, Pristina-Klina is the road towards Pec. And on that entire day, on the 29th of April, I was within these two units. Lozica and Klina are -- well, let me give an estimate now without a map, about a hundred kilometres away from Djakovica, perhaps a bit less.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Of course 100 kilometres in war conditions is a lot more than in peacetime; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is right but there is no way that on the 29th I was in the area that you referred to a few moments ago on the basis of the statement of Witness Nike Peraj.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you remember, General, where you were on the 28th of April, on the previous day? Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 28th of April, I remember that because that was the day after the day of statehood in Pristina where -- when I met with most of the commanders. And on the 28th, the leader of the group that was in Pristina, Colonel Filipovic, asked me to visit those smaller units in the morning hours, there were 11 or 12 of them, and also to receive a humanitarian organization Kolo Srpkih Sestara, so that on the 28th I spent that day in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did your command move on the 28th?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The corps command moved on the 28th from the wider region of Kisnica and Gracanica Lake towards the urban part of the town of Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we please have P2227 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: P2297.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- That's the war log of the Military Police Battalion. And could we please first look at the date, the 28th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And could you tell us when the move took place, did you participate in it, and did you go anywhere after that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's page 11 in e-court, Your Honours, that's in the English version and in B/C/S we need to see the entry for the 28th of April and then it continues on to page 12. The 28th I think -- what we need in English is on page 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: It says here, General, the Pristina Corps command moved from Kisnica to the day care centre in Pristina, and Captain Stankovic was pulled out and assigned to security. Could you explain to us when that happened and whether you were present.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to say that the 52nd Military Police Battalion was designed to provide the personal security of the corps commander and the command, and that is why this duty is listed here in the war log. The move of the part of the command started in the early morning hours, it was dark, and it was completed by around 6.00 p.m. To a building between the law school and the day care centre, it's in a neighbourhood in Pristina. Naturally, I was there and so was part of the operational units. And after that I went out to visit those structures located in the broader Pristina town region, in accordance with the request of Colonel Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you say the 28th of April during the air-strikes, you say between the day care centre and the law school. The day care centre was not opened, there were no children there, right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the education system wasn't working at the time. The law school wasn't open, but this was a building -- it was an outbuilding of the law school.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, when we're talking about this document, before the first break you told us that the command post would move about quite often.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have next page both in B/C/S and in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you look at the entry for the 1st of -- I'm sorry, I'm sorry, I apologise. While we're on the 28th here in the Military Police Battalion log-book, it is registered that a soldier was killed at Ramoc?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would like to draw Your Honours' attention, this is an incident that a witness will be called here to testify, Witness Antic, that is -- that was part of the Meja action.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Please now look at the 1st of May, it appears that at that time you were already reconnoitering a new command post in the Obilic area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have the 1st of May.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct, a team from the corps command and from the Military Police Battalion, on my orders, had already started looking for a location for the next command post, and as soon as they found it they checked it, there was another move. So this is part of the answer that I gave at our previous session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
