utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, we saw the 28th and the 29th of April. Now, what about the 27th of April, do you know where you were and what was going on on that day?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 27th of April, in Pristina, there was a modest celebration of the day of the statehood of Yugoslavia in Pristina in the presence of the 3rd Army commander and some of the subordinate commanders who had come to attend this modest celebration.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And where was that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember now, but it was one of the buildings now the Temporary Executive Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, but where? In what town?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, having seen this document dated the 29th, we veered off our original topic. Could you please tell me whether you ever removed any brigade commander or any officer from his post because of any omissions, any errors done in the process of command in terms of the performance of their service, so not because of a crime but because of such omissions?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I personally am concerned as the corps commander, I did do that. My subordinate commanders did that too at their level, the 3rd Army commander did that. I mentioned the 3rd Army commander because he was the one to remove some of the officers that were in the Pristina Corps, primarily in the units that did not belong to the Pristina Corps according to the establishment, those units that had been attached or resubordinated to the Pristina Corps. And to make myself completely clear and accurate, as early as in the beginning of April, I removed from his post a commander of the 58th Light Infantry Brigade which was stationed in the wider region of the Zecani, Zubanj Potok [as interpreted]; and I appointed a new commander and I removed from the post, the Chief of Staff of one of the battalions several commanders and artillery battalion commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, now I would like us to look at 5D531 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 533.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us very briefly what this document is all about, it is a document dated the 28th of April, and then we will move on to another document but this one is related to the one. Could you please explain to us what this is.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war from the military security department in the Pristina Corps I received some raw data about some omissions or deficiencies in the work of the commander of the 175th Infantry Brigade from the Nis Corps that had been resubordinated to the Pristina Corps. And I demanded from the commander of that brigade to send me a report in writing, indicating which of these allegations were true and which were not. In this report from the brigade commander, he claims that all the reports that he is sending to the corps command, that these reports were all accurate, that the information about his omissions in the performance of his duties were -- is incorrect, and that he was prepared to be controlled and checked in every way. That's the date is the 28th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And what did you do after you received this memo?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believed my subordinate brigade commander, not only in terms of this written report, but as far as I can remember on the 1st of May in the afternoon I went to inspect this unit, although I had already inspected this unit several times, to verify on the spot the accuracy of the allegations made by the military security organs and in this report. Let me just mention that General Pavkovic, the army commander, headed out together with me and we toured most of the units in this brigade together.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please have 5D388.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And since you've already explained this thing to us, could you just make a very brief comment indicating that this document concerns your visit and the order to carry out immediately an analysis of the situation. So that's 5D388.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a document that I drafted the next day, following the visit to this brigade together with the 3rd Army commander, and I sent it -- I addressed it to the brigade commander in question. And as the corps commander, I was not happy with the situation that I encountered there in terms of the organization of the life and work in the unit, I was unhappy with some tactical measures, and I was particularly unhappy with the personal appearance of the troops in the brigade. I ordered that additional measures be taken immediately to eliminate those deficiencies, to make a complex plan for the elimination of those deficiencies, and to monitor the implementation of all the tasks that had been given during the control. I sent a similar document to all the other commanders on the very same day as a preventive measure, as a warning regarding what the army commander and myself noticed on our visit to that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this warning is Exhibit 5D387.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me what happened to this brigade commander? Did he send you a report? Did he keep his post? Or what happened?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite soon after the 1st and the 2nd of May, the 3rd Army commander ordered the Nis Corps commander - this was the corps that was superior to this unit in accordance with the establishment - to send a team down there and to assist the Pristina Corps command to get a more detailed picture of the situation in the brigade. As far as I remember, a couple days later, the army commander and myself, we went to visit this unit again. The situation had improved regarding some of the elements, but we were still not happy with all the measures that had been taken. The army commander then decided to remove from his post the commander of that brigade. And 17 other officers from this brigade were removed from their posts, the security organ, the Chief of Staff, and some of the commanders of the battalions and artillery battalions. And other officers were appointed to those posts from the Nis Corps of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, did you take other additional measures in order to maintain the reputation of the Army of Yugoslavia and in order to prevent any kind of non-military-like behaviour, unsoldier-like behaviour?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when we're talking about measures, there is a whole set of measures. Here we can see personnel measures, but by your leave, Your Honours, I would like to say that the personnel measures were accompanied by disciplinary measures and even criminal prosecution. Let me just make a quick digression, Your Honours, when I said that I personally removed the commander of the 58th Brigade, during the war he was prosecuted, criminally prosecuted, and also disciplinary measures were taken against him for the acts he committed during the war. But now let me be more specific. Disciplinary measures were taken, military disciplinary measures were taken before the military disciplinary tribunal and criminal prosecutions were conducted in addition to personnel measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We will come to who was in charge of that and how it was done quite soon, but let me just ask you. In some situations where you observed unsoldier-like behaviour, did you insist on further medical and psychological vetting of those soldiers, additional exams?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a measure which is one of the command measures. These are not measures of responsibility, but they are highly significant for the prevention of deviant behaviour by individual members due to the stress of war. And several of my orders were issued to send both privates and officers for evaluation of their fitness at the level of the military medical commission, at the level of the 3rd Army and the Nis Corps, and the units and quite a few of their members to have their ability and fitness to carry out these difficult tasks evaluated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that's 5D315.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did the subordinate units, pursuant to your warnings, take any measures to secure order and discipline?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, although this issue is not dealt with in the set of questions dealing with the respect for humanitarian law, we made an assessment that order and discipline are a prerequisite, we made that assessment in the corps command. So several orders issued by the corps command had to do with demands that combat discipline be ensured at any cost, as I said in my orders; that is, using all available means and measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, let's look at 5D554 dated the 2nd of May after your inspection, and let's look at items 5 and 7, in view of your previous order, and then we will just refer to other examples for the benefit of the Chamber. We see here taking measures in the spirit of the order issued, and then it seems in item 5 you are being informed that security is improving with the establishment of control.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The brigade of this -- the commander of this brigade, 175th Brigade, in which these inspections were carried out, as soon as on the 2nd of May, informed me that he was acting on the orders that had been issued. And in item 5, he reports that the first measures have been implemented, that there were disciplinary and criminal prosecutions, and that this was having a positive effect on the behaviour of members of the unit. And according to the brigade commander, measures would be taken to persevere in the implementation of this task.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: On the following page, item 7, rear, paragraph 3, it seems that a list of confiscating property and motor vehicles has been drawn up, and you are being asked to send a commission for the take-over of the same.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is an even more specific response to His Honour's question. The units implemented each of these orders, complied with them, and they're reporting to the corps command that a commission should arrive to take over because the brigade commander is not authorised to proceed further as regards war booty.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm doing my best to complete my examination-in-chief before the break, so I will just give you a reference, 5D1182, 5D798, and 5D550.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, in the units of the Pristina Corps who dealt with detecting and prosecuting perpetrators of crimes and with crime prevention?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was three structures, so to speak, at the corps level which had this important task which was significant for the defence of the country, that's in the system of command from the corps command to the subordinate commands, both as regards normative regulation and as regards instituting proceedings against perpetrators of criminal offences and crimes. That's the first structure. The second structure is the organs of the military security service and the units of the military police within the scope of the corps and the brigades ex officio, because they had special powers in this area. And thirdly, the military judiciary organs established in the war, the military prosecutor's office, and the military corps at the Pristina Military District and the Pristina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, what was your attitude as the corps commander of the Pristina Corps to military courts and the military prosecutor's offices at the corps and at the military district and what were your powers over them?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military prosecutor's office and the military courts at the level of the corps, the army, and the Supreme Command Staff were an integral part of the civilian judiciary and prosecutor's office at the level of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And starting from these legal provisions, as the corps commander I had no powers whatsoever from the viewpoint of subordination, issuing orders, or asking them to do things they were not competent to do. It was my duty to create the technical and material conditions for these military judiciary organs, to perform their constitutional and legal duty, in compliance with their powers and authority. They were not part of the system of subordination in the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: As I understood it, detecting suspects or suspected perpetrators of crimes and gathering evidence was done by the security organs and the military police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They did this based on information received from the subordinate commands, other information they acquired. What I want to say is that if the subordinate commands observed something, they were duty-bound to secure the traces, to secure the crime scene, and then the military judiciary organs would become involved. And the military security organs were autonomously and independently those who had to detect, prosecute, and prevent perpetrators of crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, in the war, were there individuals in the corps units who failed to comply with the orders and instructions we have just seen or those who committed crimes?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, in spite of numerous orders and warnings, numerous measures taken by the organs of command in the course of the war, there were individuals who committed certain crimes against the army and against civilians from the standpoint of violations of international humanitarian law. I'm referring primarily to thefts of property, looting, violating dignity and morals, and all the way to murders of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: How were these crimes reported on in the units and were there attempts to hush up these reports?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These three structures that I mentioned which took measures to detect, prevent, and prosecute perpetrators of crimes also reported. So the chain of command had its system of reporting through daily or interim combat reports. Furthermore, the organs of the military security service had their own chain of reporting to the superior service of military security and the military judiciary organs and the judiciary organs, so they had two lines of reporting. They had to report to the higher military judiciary organs as well. I think you asked me something else. There was another subquestion. I'm not sure whether I have answered everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We'll come back to that later. I'll put that question to you again later on. But now tell us whether during the war when from your assistant for legal affairs you received reports, did you send reports on the crimes that had been perpetrated to your subordinate units for their information?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 5D1290, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg Your Honours' leave, I've just remembered that question I forgot to answer, whether there were any attempts to hush up crimes. I think that was your second question. I assert categorically that to the best of my knowledge, according to what I know personally and the reports arriving in the corps command, there was no hushing up of crimes committed by members of the Pristina Corps. And what you just asked me about, that was the system of command and prevention. When we received specific information about certain criminal offences or failure to comply with orders, the corps command would send -- would send a circular letter to all subordinate units, warning them and ordering them and telling them what happened, which should not have happened in certain units, and demanding that additional measures be taken. So that in spite of the fact that the chaos of war prevailed everywhere, actions should be reduced to the smallest possible measure, actions which were not fit for a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Please look at the bottom of the page. This is a survey of the information received up to the 14th of May which you received as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the military court at the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes but it's Captain Surbatovic, who compiled this information, he is the assistant to the commander for legal affairs. And as we can see, in fact, crimes of murder, theft, and aggravated theft, there are about a hundred -- well, criminal reports, I do apologise and reports for failure to implement orders, refusal to implement orders, refusal to carry out tasks in combat. There are some 20 such reports, and 14 criminal reports for murder, one officer, one non-commissioned officer, 12 privates, 26 criminal reports for theft, and 71 for aggravated theft. As we can read this for ourselves, just tell us what was the aim of sending this as a circular letter to inform all the subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is concrete information. No names are mentioned because proceedings had not been finalised in the course of the war names of perpetrators were also included in such information. And the general aim was, by means of information of this kind, to additionally get the units to undertake all possible measures, to prevent similar crimes in their units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, you just mentioned concrete. Well, let's look at 5D130. Can we please take a look at this exhibit, and here on the 15th information on crime among professional soldiers, from the corps command, and let's look at the very end of this document signed by you, where it says, unlike in the previous document, that perpetration of these and similar crimes by officers and non-commissioned officers in wartime conditions is deviant behaviour, threatening the morale and combat-readiness of the units, and there is no need even to mention the effect on the subordinates. And this also greatly diminishes the reputation of the Yugoslav Army and the confidence it enjoys among the people. And on the following page you say that you consider it indispensable that all legally prescribed measures should be taken against the perpetrators in order to prevent such behaviour, and that such perpetrators -- that the organs of the military police and the military prosecutor's offices should be immediately informed of the names of such perpetrators. So was the purpose of this information to prevent future crimes and to induce the units to comply with your orders?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a specific order, and information and also a warning as you say, and it refers to 91 members of the corps. These are not privates. These are professionals, officers and non-commissioned officers, who committed various offences, unprofessional behaviour, crimes, failure to comply with the regulations and with orders. And I say that this is a disgrace, both for the perpetrators and those around them, and I demand that stricter sanctions be implemented, especially as regards officers because I always demanded that officers give -- set an example personally. So this is for purposes of prevention, warning, to make sure that there would be as few crimes and as few dishonourable actions committed in that wartime as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, the military judiciary organs during the course of the war, did they take -- did they initiate proceedings against persons unknown, even when there were no indications to the effect that any members of the Army of Yugoslavia were involved in those crimes?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that both prosecution offices filed quite a few criminal reports against perpetrators unknown with a general objective in mind, that crimes do not go unpunished, do not remain outside the realm of justice, regardless of who committed these crimes, and regardless of the fact that there was no evidence in terms of the perpetrators being members of the military. These measures were taken in order to prevent any crimes from being concealed, crimes that were committed during the course of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know approximately what the number of criminal reports filed was in respect of those crimes that constitute violations of international humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that during the state of war and during the period in the immediate aftermath of the war, there were about 245 criminal reports that deal with violations of international humanitarian law. 20 criminal reports out of these had to do with murder, five for assaults against integrity and morale, and the remainder, 200-something, had to do with property-related issues, looting, theft, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, tours of inspection from the security administration, we saw that on the 4th and 5th of May, General Farkas in the beginning of June, General Vasiljevic, did they familiarise the command of the Pristina Corps that there were some omissions and failures in terms of the reporting of crime? Did they tell you about that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to respond in very concrete terms that as for the first arrival of the chief of the security administration of the Supreme Command Staff, General Geza Farkas, initially I did not know that he had come to the 3rd Army within the Pristina Corps and I did not meet up with him, I did not see a report on his tour and inspection, and I did not have occasion to hear what you refer to just now, that in the corps command he indicated some failures or omissions in reporting. I am not challenging. Perhaps he said that to the late Colonel Antic or Colonel Stojanovic from the command of the Pristina Corps. However, I repeat that as for failures and omissions on the part of the corps command I was not informed about that from this team. Maybe I shouldn't be referring to a team, maybe he was there on his own, because I really do not know who it was who was there with him. As for the second part of your question, it pertained to the arrival of the team in the beginning of June, the one that was headed by General Vasiljevic. I did have information to the effect that this team was touring the military police units and the military security organs, and that all of this was evolving according to plan; but yet again I say that I did not meet up with this team except in the basement of the Grand Hotel for 20 minutes. From this team I did not receive any warnings in terms of there indeed being some omissions or failures in the process of reporting, and my assistant commander for security in the corps, Colonel Stojanovic, did not inform me of any serious objections. With the permission of the Trial Chamber, I wish to say that Vasiljevic, who was a Prosecution witness here, confirmed that here. I'm just speaking of my own personal experience in this regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, you say except for these 20 minutes in June, or rather, did that happen on the 1st of June, 1999?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would be around then.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You heard that yourself here, but now I'm going to ask you whether this was a meeting of some Joint Command or what was this occasion when you saw General Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that sometime in the afternoon hours the army commander said that we should go to town, to Pristina, to our information centre, and that there we would meet some people, that we were supposed to hear some information about the diplomatic initiative of our country that was underway in terms of bringing the war to the end. To be quite frank, I did not know that I would meet up with General Vasiljevic then. I actually didn't even know him before that. So it was no Joint Command. May I say it was the army commander and myself who were there; I was right next to him in the same vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And who else was present in that room, can you recall?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in that room in the evening hours in one of the corners -- well, it was this information centre, the group of officers from the General Staff, from the 3rd Army and the corps, the central part, there was the army commander, there was I, the chief of security of the corps from the military. I don't know whether anyone else was there. There was this team of people who I did not know. Later on I found out that this was General Vasiljevic and Gajic. Then two state officials came up, Mr. Sainovic and Andjelkovic, briefly. They said hello, greeted everyone, they said what was said. Some people went to dinner, other people went back to their units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You say that you then saw Mr. Sainovic. When did you last see him, if you can remember, before that day, the 1st of June, 1999?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Along with an apology to the Trial Chamber, I think -- no, I'm sure that somebody from the MUP was present there as well, because we met up, and we talked about these problems of ours; and it was only later that these two gentlemen came up. Could you please remind me specifically what it was that you asked me, this last bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Let me ask you that at the end. Let me ask you before that, you said there were some discussions about the agreement. Are you referring to the Military Technical Agreement, and after that did you take part, and how many days later, in the realization of the Kumanova Agreement, the Military Technical Agreement, and when was that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the introduction to the Military Technical Agreement. I heard concrete information then from Mr. Sainovic that the Russian representative, Chernomyrdin, was in Belgrade for a few days and that some draft was being prepared of a broader international agreement on the cessation of war activities. On the 5th of June already, I was in the area of Djeneral Jankovic, on the opposite end, at the border towards Macedonia. At that time I did not know that I was appointed member of the negotiating team. I was there on my own, and I came back to carry out this special operation of the withdrawal of the Pristina Corps from the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, this question that you asked me to repeat was as follows: Before the 1st of June, can you remember when it was that you had last seen Mr. Sainovic? Did you ever see him in 1999?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I saw him perhaps on TV. I think there was this information that he had come to Pristina, that he negotiated to and talked to Rugova, but I did not have occasion to see him before this date, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you remember that you perhaps saw him before the war began, before the bombing started?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, before the bombing started, he was head of the state commission for cooperation with the OSCE mission, and until the 20th of March I did see him a few times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this a suitable time for us to interrupt you, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, I thought that ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we shall break for 30 minutes and resume at ten to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, in the war in 1999, were there any clear-up operations carried out of the field, of the battle-field; and if yes, what did those clear-up operations comprise?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The clear-up of the ground and of the battle-fields was done in Kosovo and Metohija. It is a complex set of sanitary and hygienic measures, sanitary technical measures, and other measures designed to locate the wounded and dead, people who were wounded or killed in the war, to locate any ordnance, and to remove this ordnance in a way that would not endanger the population and the environment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were any clear-up operations carried out to remove the threat of radioactive ammunition and cluster bombs as part of those operations?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By your leave, Your Honours, I would like to say that clear-up operations during the war in Kosovo and Metohija went beyond the requirements as they're set out in the Rules of Logistic Support because this activity is part of logistics. In light of the nature of the war, this was one of the most asymmetrical wars ever fought. In light of the fact that all kinds of ordnance, including state-of-the-art ordnance that we were not familiar with, clear-up operations were very important, extremely important, something that the corps command and the subordinate really focused on, and it comprised the clear-up, the removal, of radioactive ammunition. This meant that after every long-range strike or any air-strike, special teams and units of the Pristina Corps, those that dealt with atomic, chemical, and biological defence were dispatched urgently to locate the target site, to control whether there were -- to check whether there was any radiation, to put up signs around it, to warn the civilian population, and to do other measures involving the units to prevent any damage caused by radiation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to draw Your Honours' attention to 5D311 and 5D182, these two documents deal with this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were any clear-up operations carried out to remove any mines or explosives that may have been planted by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, definitely. This was a particular problem for the military personnel and for the civilian population, the mines that were laid by the armed rebel forces. The situation was made even more complex by the use of tens of thousands of special mines, the cluster mines or the cluster bombs, that were dropped by NATO aeroplanes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 5D367.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: This is the 5th of April. You order that any such explosive devices, mines should be located and destroyed.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a specific order from the Pristina Corps command to the commander of the 15th Armoured Brigade, because some mines and explosives had been found in the towns of Klina and Glogovac. The corps command then ordered that the brigade should set up specialised groups to remove any mines or explosives from those axes in order to avoid any casualties, both in the corps and the police units, but also among the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Now I would like us to look at Exhibit 5D355. As early as on the 1st of April, did you order that signs should be put up visibly around those locations where there were cluster bombs or bomblets or around the areas where mines had been laid?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to tell you, Your Honours, that the corps command did not have the military know-how about this -- these banned weapons, cluster bombs. Some information had come from the General Staff, but this kind of weapon caused great danger, great risk to everybody moving around Kosovo and Metohija, and this was an effort on the part of the Pristina Corps command to do everything whenever those weapons were found, this ordnance was found, the so-called yellow killers, that those sites should be marked, as indicated here, with plastic tape to protect the civilian population and then to destroy this ordnance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, who launched the initiative to engage forensic medicine experts from the military medical academy in the clear-up operations?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we please look at Exhibit 5D383.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, Your Honours, I will be speaking in the first-person singular because as an officer, I was familiar with the basic provisions about the clear-up operations on the ground and of the battle-fields. But when the war broke out in Kosovo, I and the corps command and the army command, in fact, we realized that there could be catastrophic consequences for all those who happened to be in that area. And I personally made this decision, and I asked from the army command and the Supreme Command Staff, I asked them to send pathologists, forensic medicine experts to assist the corps units in this complex effort to clear-up the terrain because there were such horrors to be seen. It was impossible to identify some of the members of the police -- of the corps that had been killed. Mistakes had been made when identifying remains, and my idea was to use those experts while we're under attack by NATO air-strikes and the terrorist forces to identify all the remains that could be identified, to do everything to prevent any cover-ups of any crimes committed by both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Here we see on the screen the chief of the medical service is writing to the Pristina Corps command. It says here: "Pursuant to your telegram of the 26th of April referring to the engagement of a forensic pathologist so that ..."

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to say that even before this date I had demanded from the army command, and on the 20th of April a single military pathologist from the military hospital in Nis had already been dispatched to the Pristina Corps command to be a member of this special team for the clear-up of the ground and battle-fields. And this is a new request to the 3rd Army command and the Supreme Command Staff for further deployment of those forensic medicine specialists.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, we've seen that one of the 26th of March [as interpreted]. I think that in May you asked for some additional teams, just as you've just explained to us -- well, I'm not going to -- I'm just going to ask you whether this was in order to cover up any crimes or, rather, to discover any crimes.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By your leave, Your Honours, I would like to say once again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've already answered that question by telling us it was to avoid cover-up by either party. I think for the avoidance of any doubt, line 10 on page 66 should be the 26th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, it should read the 26th of April and not March. Let me give you a reference for the second request, that's 5D421.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, in Kosovo and Metohija was there a plan, were you aware of such a plan for the deportation and forcible transfer of Albanian civilians from Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before this Trial Chamber, speaking under an oath, as I have been for several days now, I can categorically state that there was no plan that the corps command or its subordinate units knew of or participated in or got from their superiors, so absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you from your subordinate units in the field receive any information about the local population feeling fear and being concerned about the air-strikes and that this resulted in them fleeing their homes. And could I please have 5D1210 up on the screen while we wait for your answer.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corps command did receive reports as part of the combat reports. There were also some special reports in which the subordinate commanders were noting the problem of the migrations of the civilian population, the civilian population moving out, which was the result of NATO attacks and large-scale destruction and large number of casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, we have yet to receive a translation for this document. Could you please read item 3.4, morale, this is Opolje Tactical Group command, the date is the 8th of May, could you please read what it says here in item 4, the state of morale.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a regular combat report from the Opolje Tactical Group it was at the extreme left wing at Dragas plateau where the brigade commander reports that among the local population there is concern and fear of the air-strikes, and this is reflected in them fleeing their homes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it appropriate to mention at this point, Mr. Bakrac, that the Defence objected to the admission of similar evidence at the hand of the Prosecution, the evidence in the form of reports by Human Rights Watch and the OSCE; and therefore, you should be on notice that this sort of material is unlikely to be given much, if any, weight as indicative of the reaction of the population to NATO air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is a combat report from the field, and let me ask the General.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know what is the basis for the inclusion of this information in the combat reports on the part of your subordinate units, if you know; if you don't know -- did they talk to the people in the -- on the ground?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I visited this tactical group in May, and I personally met those people, Goranis, Muslims, Turks in that area. I spoke to this commander and to other commanders. He wrote this because he had spoken to people, he had seen this. And I as a first-hand participant in the war, I myself experienced this, I saw this, I heard this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, I'm staggered that you should await my intervention before you lead that evidence from the witness. And you should have up until that point been relying on something which was obviously on the face of it of no different value from the evidence of what people said to OSCE and Human Rights Watch interviewers. Now, I'm not clear still about the question whether any of these people were Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this document is indicative of the state of mind of the accused and of the others as to what actually was going on and what the cause may have been for the movements of the population. This is what this document intends to show.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, did you have any information as to whether the KLA moved civilians and sent them, or rather, sent to NATO information about their whereabouts and guided NATO to targets of the VJ and MUP?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had not only precise operative information about this tactic and strategy by forces of the armed rebellion, but we also had numerous events and occurrences and facts confirming that there were NATO air-strikes after this information had been given to them and targets on the ground marked for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that's 5D1312.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you have any information showing that in some cases there was an inter-ethnic conflict on a local level which might have been the cause for the movement of civilians?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were reports arriving from parts of units where the commanders reported that persons unknown in civilian clothes or wearing parts of some sort of uniform were committing criminal offences against property in the villages, that they were torching houses, looting. And if I may draw a conclusion and make an assessment, this would certainly have had an effect on the movement, migration, and displacement of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see 5D546 dated the 24th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you comment on this document?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a combat report from the command of the 175th Infantry Brigade, reporting to the corps command and informing them that there was torching of houses and looting perpetrated by local people and that there had been an intervention by the Military Police Company of the brigade in the village of Cernica in order to discover the persons committing crimes and arrest them. These were local inhabitants of the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are we on the correct page for this?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's in item 2, Your Honours, the second paragraph under item 2, and it begins with: "After dismissing most of the volunteers and the establishment of control over the territory, there has been more burning of houses and thefts by the locals." In the English version it's somewhere in the middle of item 2, after "dismissing most of the volunteers ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And do you know how many people were arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in this combat report, no, but there are combat reports from this same unit where on one occasion they arrested six civilians who perpetrated such offences, handed them over to the organs of the interior; and in another report it says that together with organs of the MUP they were chasing such persons and that the unit had arrested four persons with weapons. That's all I can say with certainty at present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were these Serb civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. With respect to this unit, they were Serb civilians from the area, they were locals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were they part of the civil defence or civil protection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. These were locals who were not in the defence system and the structures of the defence system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could they be described as armed non-Siptars?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those who did the torching and looting in these reports, I didn't find that they were armed but that they stole and looted, yes, and that they were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've just said the unit had arrested four persons with weapons. That was on a different occasion, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On a different occasion, yes, and if you wish that's in a different context. I can tell you if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So these were civilians who unarmed were setting fire to the homes of whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Albanian houses in the villages of Cernica, Zegra, Koretiste, and I can't recall the names of the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And were these occupied or unoccupied houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the reports it doesn't say. I can only make assumptions I'm inclined to believe they were not occupied at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, were there a large number of civilian buildings damaged by NATO air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, from what I know from my personal inspection and my survey of the documentation, there were many buildings in Kosovo and Metohija, some socially owned, some privately owned, which were destroyed. Even entire villages on the Pastrik-Prizren axis were razed to the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, 72 -- page 72, line 2, the witness said: Many hundreds of buildings have been destroyed in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I'm coming to the end of my examination. Tell me, in 1998, as we saw, you were the Chief of Staff of the Pristina Corps and spent most of your time at the forward command post in Djakovica. Did you ever attend any meetings in Belgrade in 1998? Did you go to Belgrade at all?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't even see Belgrade in 1998, nor did I attend any meeting of any organs or institutions in the capital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And in 1999?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go there in 1999 either. When the war's practically finished on the 16th of June, the day -- the Army Day of Yugoslavia, even then I did not attend the central celebrations in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, I have just one more document, it dates from the year 2001, and we have heard many times and questions about it were put here, there was certain doubts as to whether there was something called a Joint Command in 1998 and 1999. First I will ask you and we'll put on the screen 5D475. In March 2001 what was the position you held in the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In March 2001 I was the commander of the 3rd Army of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were there attempts at the time to establish -- to establish coordinated or joint forces of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only were there such attempts, but pursuant to a decision of the president of the FRY a coordination body for the south of Serbia was established, which is still in existence, and the so-called joint security forces were established from the army and the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And what was your response to the establishment or the attempt to establish joint security forces, or rather, a temporary Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the decision of the president of the FRY dated the 8th of March, 2001, it was envisaged that part of the forces of the 3rd Army and part of the forces of the MUP should be subordinated to a coordinating body for the south of Serbia in carrying out combat tasks for the defence of the integrity of the country in the south of Serbia on the territory of three municipalities where the terrorist forces numbering over 3 and a half thousand were threatening the integrity of the state. I responded to that fact. I reacted to the fact that forces of the army were being subordinated to a civilian organ and that a civilian organ should be in command of part of the units of the 3rd Army, which is contrary to Article 3 of the Law on the Army of Yugoslavia. I demanded from the Chief of the General Staff that through the president of the FRY I should be replaced from my duty because as an officer I did not wish to participate in the setting of a precedent violating the system of command with reference to the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And, General, to avoid reading the whole of paragraph 2, you have just explained this now, but you also said that this would create a precedent in the functioning of the system of command. In your letter you wrote that this would constitute a precedent in the functioning of the command system. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be more precise, this is not a letter, it is an application to be relieved of the duty of commander of the 3rd Army. And when I use the term "precedent," what I meant to say was for the first time since I became an officer, I was in a situation where someone not authorised by the constitution and the laws should be in command of part of the 3rd Army where there are casualties because --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the numbers, numbers of soldiers who had been killed and wounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number of soldiers you referred to there as having been killed or wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, up to that point in time, eight soldiers from the Pristina Corps of the 3rd Army had been killed and 52 wounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, you said that this would constitute a precedent in the system of command and that never before had any Joint Command existed, which would include civilians.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may be allowed to say this, I addressed the Chief of the General Staff and the president of the state to say that in my entire military career this was the first time I had seen that someone who was unauthorised - and that would be the coordinating body for the south of Serbia - is put in a position to command my army. I did not agree to this, even if it meant my being dismissed from my duty and taking off the uniform I had on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And, General, my last question: How did President Kostunica respond to this request of yours?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Mr. Kostunica, was informed by General Pavkovic, the Chief of the General Staff and he received me and the commander of the Pristina Corps, General Stevanovic saying he was not prepared to carry out such tasks and allow a precedent to be set in the chain of command and the chief of the General Staff. When he heard my oral explanation of what you see written here on the screen, he said why did we do this. He wondered why he signed that order. He did not accept my application to be relieved of my duty. He gave me the task of returning to the army command, and very soon his decision was changed. So the units of the Pristina Corps and the 3rd Army were restored to the command of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, these were all my questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Just one matter, Mr. Lazarevic. Why does the coordinating body for the south of Serbia still exist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in that part of area which is called the south of Serbia there are three municipalities. The situation there is still unstable politically and in terms of security, and this is still affected by the situation in Kosovo and Metohija. There are some political demands that this area which they refer to as eastern Kosovo be annexed to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But do you know whether the MUP are subordinated to the coordinating body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, I attended a number of meetings of the coordinating body. I am not aware of them being subordinated and I do not know whether they tried in this way to resolve this problem. This is unconstitutional possible use, but I'm saying this specifically in respect to the 3rd Army that was under my command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Do Defence counsel -- Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll be very brief, believe me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Lazarevic, General, you mentioned that in 1998, together with your commander - I assume that was General Pavkovic - you were at at least three meetings that you participated in together with your commander and four civilians Minic, Andjelkovic, Matkovic, and Sainovic and some representatives of the MUP. First question that I would like to put to you: Could you say approximately how many people attended these meetings, roughly? It's not a question of one or two more or less.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was 10 to 12, a biggish group I would say when I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please answer briefly. Was it always the same people or did they change?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I want to correct something, please. I did not say that the four persons you mentioned to me just now were present in each and every one of these situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So I may conclude that it wasn't always the same people who were present, that the persons present changed.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. You are a special witness, General. You heard the entire trial in an unpleasant position, that is to say that of the accused. You were Chief of Staff of the Pristina Corps and the commander was General Pavkovic. You heard the testimony of General Simic, who was the Chief of Staff of the 3rd Army. Now, I just want to remind you of a few things. I don't think that is going to be a problem. He said that General Pavkovic came to see him in the evening, to get commands, and then with the command he would go to this meetings -- these meetings, and then he would coordinate with the MUP. If the MUP had any special requirements he would go back to General Simic and he would give him a definite decision regardless of whether he accepted it or did not accept it. So the conclusion is General Simic said: I am the one who issues orders, Pavkovic, that's the law. My question is as follows. You were the second-ranking person in the Pristina Corps. Is that how things worked, as General Simic said?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My knowledge really and truly confirms an even more rigorous approach by General Samardzic and Simic. Quite simply, they did not allow the smallest unit of 200 or 250 men, the rank of a combat group, to be on the move without their explicit written orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, this question you've just been asked is very particular to circumstances about which we heard evidence. Are you able to help us on this particular question? Because it presupposes that you knew all about the activities of General Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I didn't ask him whether he knew everything about General Pavkovic's activities. I'm talking about the forward command post of the Pristina Corps. Did General Pavkovic receive orders from General Simic? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But, Mr. Fila, your question was that General Pavkovic would come to see Simic in the evening and get commands, and then with the command he would go to these meetings. So this presupposes that this witness, Mr. Lazarevic, knows that these meetings were taking place and that General Pavkovic was going there as some intermediate stage between implementing the instructions of Simic. Now, do you know about these circumstances so that you can help us precisely with what was -- about what was going on between Pavkovic and Simic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, I personally did not attend a single meeting at the forward command post of the 3rd Army in Pristina; however, I did have information and I did have knowledge. The corps commander personally told me that he went there, that there were evening briefings at the forward command post of the 3rd Army to General Simic and to General Samardzic. And what I testified to a few moments ago I'm saying through numerous orders that I saw even at the forward command post in Djakovica, what was written by General Simic and by General Samardzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, I understand that. But did you also know that General Pavkovic was going to other meetings which may have involved people who were jointly coordinating activity, whether commanding it or not? Were you aware of him going to these meetings after he had spoken to Simic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, I did have information that General Pavkovic with a group of officers from the corps command, together with colleagues from the MUP, talked about coordination and activities in concert. I also had information that he went to Belgrade together with the commander of the 3rd Army to see General Perisic. He personally told me that when he toured the forward command post in Djakovica. I, on a few occasions attended, together with him, these meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The foundation for this question that I put is at the very outset that he was present at three such meetings and that is why I asked him that, very simple.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: General, you described the content of these meetings as you did, and you said just now that there was some information there, mutual information, coordination with the MUP and the army. I'm interested in the following. After these three meetings or perhaps four, never mind, after October 1998 until the end of the war, did you ever attend a meeting where some kind of coordination was made and where civilians were present, regardless of whether it was called Joint Command or not? What matters to me is whether civilians were there.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally did not attend a single of these later meetings, and really and truly I do not have any knowledge of the corps commander having this kind of coordinated activity with people from the MUP because the focus was on activities of cooperation with the OSCE.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll have to break there, Mr. Fila. I know it's an unnatural way of doing things, but we have no option I'm afraid because I think the court is occupied this afternoon. So we shall adjourn until tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 13th day of November, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24
